# APIs, HTTP and REST {#sec-ch-api-rest}

> *"REST is a hybrid style derived from several of the network-based
> architectural styles…"* — Roy T. Fielding, 2000 [@fielding2000, §5.1]

```{python}
#| echo: false
import apibook as ab
ab.setup()
import json, math, sys, time
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- explain what an **API** is and how a **web API** works on top of **HTTP**:
  URLs, request and response messages, headers, status codes, JSON — down to
  the bytes on the wire, by writing a client and a server with sockets;
- use the HTTP **methods** according to their semantics, **prove** what
  safety and **idempotence** guarantee, when retries are safe ("at least once
  plus idempotent = exactly once", with its hypotheses), and how
  **exponential backoff with jitter** avoids retry storms;
- apply the **REST** constraints — resources, representations,
  statelessness, caching, hypermedia — and use HTTP **caching** and
  **conditional requests** (ETags), with the proofs that the cache's age is
  never underestimated and that `If-Match` prevents lost updates;
- design, implement, validate and document **endpoints** with FastAPI,
  Pydantic, JSON Schema and OpenAPI, with correct status codes, standard
  error documents and **pagination** that is correct under concurrent
  inserts;
- reason about an API **in production**: Little's law, tail latency under
  fan-out, rate limiting with a token bucket, and the basics of
  authentication, HTTPS, CORS and request signing.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
What an API is; the HTTP methods; REST as an architectural style for APIs;
what an endpoint is.
:::

## What an API is, and HTTP from the ground up {#sec-api-http}

### Interfaces between programs

An **API** — application programming interface — is a **contract** between
two pieces of software: what one may ask of the other, in which form, and
what it will get back. Part I used APIs from the first chapter: the functions
of a module are its API (@sec-ch-functions), and their documented behaviour
is the contract. Part II used the operating system's API, the system calls
(@sec-ch-cpp-python). A **web API** is a contract between programs that talk
over a network: a *client* sends a **request** to a *server*, which performs
it and returns a **response**. The two sides may be written in different
languages, run on different machines and be developed by different teams;
what keeps them compatible is the contract alone. That is the reason for most
of this chapter: a good web API is one whose contract is explicit, uniform
and hard to misuse.

Nearly all web APIs speak **HTTP**, the protocol of the Web. Its semantics —
methods, status codes, headers, caching — are defined in RFC 9110
[@rfc9110], independently of how messages travel: HTTP/1.1 as text over a TCP
connection [@rfc9112], HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 as binary frames over TCP and QUIC.
The semantics are what an API designer works with; the HTTP/1.1 text format
is what we look at to see them.

### Addresses: URLs

A request is addressed to a **URL**, whose syntax is defined by RFC 3986
[@rfc3986]:

```{python}
from urllib.parse import urlsplit, parse_qs, quote

url = "https://api.example.com:8443/v1/wines/42?fields=alcohol,colour&lang=en#notes"
parts = urlsplit(url)
for name in ("scheme", "hostname", "port", "path", "query", "fragment"):
    print(f"{name:9s} {getattr(parts, name)!r}")
print("query parameters:", parse_qs(parts.query))
print("percent-encoding:", quote("rosé & co"), "<- reserved and non-ASCII characters escaped")
```

The **scheme** selects the protocol (`https` = HTTP over TLS, @sec-api-production);
**host** and **port** locate the server; the **path** identifies a resource
on it; the **query** carries parameters; the **fragment** never leaves the
client. Characters that would be ambiguous — spaces, `&`, `?`, non-ASCII
letters — are **percent-encoded** as the bytes of their UTF-8 encoding.

### Messages

An HTTP/1.1 message is text: a start line, header fields `Name: value` (one
per line, names case-insensitive), an empty line, and an optional body whose
length the headers announce (`Content-Length`, or chunked encoding)
[@rfc9112, §2–6]. To see real messages, here is a small server built with the
standard library, and a client that speaks to it through a raw TCP socket —
no HTTP library at all:

```{python}
ab.write("hello_server.py", '''
    """A tiny JSON server with the standard library: GET /hello?name=..., POST /echo."""
    import json, sys
    from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
    from urllib.parse import urlsplit, parse_qs

    class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"
        def send_json(self, code, obj):
            body = json.dumps(obj).encode()
            self.send_response(code)
            self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(body)
        def do_GET(self):
            url = urlsplit(self.path)
            if url.path == "/hello":
                name = parse_qs(url.query).get("name", ["world"])[0]
                self.send_json(200, {"greeting": f"hello, {name}"})
            else:
                self.send_json(404, {"error": "no such resource"})
        def do_POST(self):
            if self.path != "/echo":
                return self.send_json(404, {"error": "no such resource"})
            data = self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0)))
            try:
                self.send_json(200, {"you_sent": json.loads(data)})
            except json.JSONDecodeError:
                self.send_json(400, {"error": "body is not JSON"})
        def log_message(self, *args):
            pass

    ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", int(sys.argv[1])), Handler).serve_forever()
''')
HELLO = [sys.executable, "hello_server.py", "{port}"]
```

```{python}
import socket

def raw_exchange(port, request: bytes) -> bytes:
    """Send bytes on a TCP connection and read the reply until the server closes it."""
    with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port)) as s:
        s.sendall(request)
        reply = b""
        while chunk := s.recv(4096):
            reply += chunk
    return reply

with ab.server("", cmd=HELLO) as base:
    port = int(base.rsplit(":", 1)[1])
    request = (b"GET /hello?name=Ada HTTP/1.1\r\n"
               b"Host: 127.0.0.1\r\n"
               b"Accept: application/json\r\n"
               b"Connection: close\r\n"
               b"\r\n")
    reply = raw_exchange(port, request)
print(request.decode().replace("\r\n", "\n"))
print(ab.mask(reply.decode()).replace("\r\n", "\n"))
```

The request line says **what** to do (`GET`), **to what** (`/hello?name=Ada`)
and in which protocol version; the `Host` header names the server (one IP
address may host many sites); `Accept` says which representation the client
prefers. The response's **status line** carries a three-digit **status
code** and a reason phrase; its headers describe the body (`Content-Type`,
`Content-Length`) and the server. `Connection: close` asked the server to
close the connection after the response; by default HTTP/1.1 keeps it open
for further requests, which is why the length of the body must be stated —
otherwise the client could not know where one response ends.

An HTTP library does all of this for us. The standard choice in this chapter
is **httpx** [@christie2026], a client with the same interface for
synchronous and asynchronous code:

```{python}
import httpx

with ab.server("", cmd=HELLO) as base:
    r = httpx.get(f"{base}/hello", params={"name": "Ada"})
    print(r.status_code, r.headers["content-type"], r.json())
    r = httpx.post(f"{base}/echo", json={"wine": 42, "scores": [0.1, 0.9]})
    print(r.status_code, r.json())
    print(httpx.post(f"{base}/echo", content=b"not json").status_code,
          httpx.get(f"{base}/nothing-here").status_code)
```

### Status codes and representations

Status codes are grouped by their first digit [@rfc9110, §15]:

| Class | Meaning | Codes an API uses most |
|---|---|---|
| 1xx | informational | 100 Continue |
| 2xx | **success** | 200 OK, 201 Created, 202 Accepted, 204 No Content |
| 3xx | **redirection** | 301/308 moved permanently, 302/307 temporarily, 304 Not Modified |
| 4xx | **client error** — retrying the same request will not help | 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 409 Conflict, 412 Precondition Failed, 415 Unsupported Media Type, 422 Unprocessable Content, 429 Too Many Requests |
| 5xx | **server error** — the request may succeed later | 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout |

The distinction between 4xx and 5xx is the first thing a client looks at: a
4xx says "fix your request", a 5xx (and 429) says "maybe try again later" —
the basis of retry policies (@sec-api-methods).

A resource can have several **representations**: the same wine as JSON, as
CSV, in English or Italian. The client states its preferences with `Accept`
and `Accept-Language`, the server chooses and says what it chose with
`Content-Type` — **content negotiation**. For APIs the representation is
almost always **JSON** [@rfc8259]: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, `true`,
`false`, `null`. Two caveats matter for numerical data: JSON has no `NaN` or
infinity (Python's `json.dumps(float("nan"))` writes `NaN`, which strict
parsers reject — use `allow_nan=False`), and many clients parse numbers as
64-bit floats, so integers beyond $2^{53}$ lose precision (send large IDs as
strings).

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-api1-http-easy}
## Easy — a request by hand
Write by hand the bytes of an HTTP/1.1 request that sends the JSON object
`{"name": "rosé"}` with `POST` to `/echo` on `127.0.0.1`, closing the
connection afterwards. What is the `Content-Length`? Then classify the status
codes 200, 201, 204, 301, 304, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, 500, 502
and 503: success, redirection, client error or server error — and which of
them justify an automatic retry?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`Content-Length` counts **bytes** of the body, not characters: `é` is two
bytes in UTF-8. Lines end with CRLF (`\r\n`) and the headers end with an
empty line.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The body `{"name": "rosé"}` has 16 characters and 17 bytes.
```{python}
from http import HTTPStatus

body = json.dumps({"name": "rosé"}, ensure_ascii=False).encode()
request = (b"POST /echo HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\n"
           + f"Content-Length: {len(body)}\r\n".encode() + b"Connection: close\r\n\r\n" + body)
print(f"{len(body.decode())} characters, {len(body)} bytes")
with ab.server("", cmd=HELLO) as base:
    print(raw_exchange(int(base.rsplit(':', 1)[1]), request).decode().split("\r\n\r\n")[1])

kind = {2: "success", 3: "redirection", 4: "client error", 5: "server error"}
for code in (200, 201, 204, 301, 304, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, 500, 502, 503):
    retry = code in (429, 502, 503, 504) or (code == 500)
    print(f"{code} {HTTPStatus(code).phrase:24s} {kind[code // 100]:13s} {'retry may help' if retry else ''}")
```
Retrying makes sense for 429 (after the delay in `Retry-After`), 502, 503
and 504 (transient failures of the server or of a gateway), and — with care,
only for idempotent requests — for 500 and for connections that broke
without a response. A 4xx other than 429 will fail identically every time.
The classic mistake is `Content-Length: len(text)` in characters: with
non-ASCII text the server waits for bytes that never come, or truncates the
body.
:::

::: {#exr-api1-http-medium}
## Medium — a client on sockets
Write `http_get(host, port, path)` with the `socket` module only: send a
`GET` with `Connection: close`, then parse the status line, the headers (into
a dictionary with lower-case keys) and the body, using `Content-Length`.
Test it against `python -m http.server` serving a directory with a JSON file,
and compare the result with httpx.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Split the reply at the first `\r\n\r\n`: before it, the status line and the
headers; after it, the body. A real client reads exactly `Content-Length`
bytes rather than waiting for the connection to close.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
def http_get(host, port, path):
    with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=5) as s:
        s.sendall(f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {host}\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n".encode())
        data = b""
        while b"\r\n\r\n" not in data:                         # read until the end of the headers
            data += s.recv(4096)
        head, body = data.split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)
        lines = head.decode("iso-8859-1").split("\r\n")
        version, code, reason = lines[0].split(" ", 2)
        headers = {}
        for line in lines[1:]:
            name, value = line.split(":", 1)
            headers[name.strip().lower()] = value.strip()      # field names are case-insensitive
        length = int(headers.get("content-length", 0))
        while len(body) < length:                              # read exactly the announced body
            body += s.recv(4096)
    return int(code), headers, body[:length]

(ab.WORK / "static").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(ab.WORK / "static" / "wine.json").write_text(json.dumps({"id": 42, "alcohol": 13.2}))
cmd = [sys.executable, "-m", "http.server", "{port}", "--bind", "127.0.0.1", "--directory", str(ab.WORK / "static")]
with ab.server("", cmd=cmd) as base:
    port = int(base.rsplit(":", 1)[1])
    code, headers, body = http_get("127.0.0.1", port, "/wine.json")
    print(code, headers["content-type"], headers["content-length"], json.loads(body))
    print(http_get("127.0.0.1", port, "/missing.json")[0])
    r = httpx.get(f"{base}/wine.json")
    print("httpx agrees:", (r.status_code, r.json()) == (code, json.loads(body)))
```
The two subtle points are the framing — the body ends after
`Content-Length` bytes, not when `recv` happens to return — and decoding the
header block as ISO-8859-1, the historical charset of HTTP header fields,
not UTF-8. A real client also handles chunked transfer encoding, redirects,
keep-alive, timeouts and TLS: reasons to use a library.
:::

::: {#exr-api1-http-hard}
## Hard — a server from scratch
Write a minimal HTTP/1.1 server with `socket` only: one thread per
connection, `GET /hello?name=...` and `POST /echo` with a JSON body (read
with `Content-Length`), and correct errors — 400 for a malformed request or
invalid JSON, 404 for an unknown path, 405 for a wrong method, 411 when a
`POST` has no `Content-Length`. Test it with `curl` and with httpx.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`socket.create_server(("127.0.0.1", port))`, then `accept()` in a loop and a
`threading.Thread` per connection. Read up to the blank line, parse, read the
body, write the response with `Content-Length` and `Connection: close`, close
the socket. A `405` response should include an `Allow` header.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
ab.write("tiny_http.py", '''
    import json, socket, sys, threading
    from urllib.parse import urlsplit, parse_qs

    REASONS = {200: "OK", 400: "Bad Request", 404: "Not Found", 405: "Method Not Allowed", 411: "Length Required"}

    def respond(conn, code, obj, extra=""):
        body = json.dumps(obj).encode()
        head = (f"HTTP/1.1 {code} {REASONS[code]}\\r\\nContent-Type: application/json\\r\\n"
                f"Content-Length: {len(body)}\\r\\n{extra}Connection: close\\r\\n\\r\\n")
        conn.sendall(head.encode() + body)

    def handle(conn):
        with conn:
            data = b""
            while b"\\r\\n\\r\\n" not in data:
                chunk = conn.recv(4096)
                if not chunk:
                    return
                data += chunk
            head, body = data.split(b"\\r\\n\\r\\n", 1)
            try:
                lines = head.decode("iso-8859-1").split("\\r\\n")
                method, target, version = lines[0].split(" ")
                headers = {k.strip().lower(): v.strip() for k, v in (l.split(":", 1) for l in lines[1:])}
            except ValueError:
                return respond(conn, 400, {"error": "malformed request"})
            url = urlsplit(target)
            routes = {"/hello": "GET", "/echo": "POST"}
            if url.path not in routes:
                return respond(conn, 404, {"error": "no such resource"})
            if method != routes[url.path]:
                return respond(conn, 405, {"error": "method not allowed"}, f"Allow: {routes[url.path]}\\r\\n")
            if method == "GET":
                name = parse_qs(url.query).get("name", ["world"])[0]
                return respond(conn, 200, {"greeting": f"hello, {name}"})
            if "content-length" not in headers:
                return respond(conn, 411, {"error": "Content-Length required"})
            n = int(headers["content-length"])
            while len(body) < n:
                body += conn.recv(4096)
            try:
                return respond(conn, 200, {"you_sent": json.loads(body[:n])})
            except (json.JSONDecodeError, UnicodeDecodeError):
                return respond(conn, 400, {"error": "body is not JSON"})

    srv = socket.create_server(("127.0.0.1", int(sys.argv[1])))
    while True:
        conn, _ = srv.accept()
        threading.Thread(target=handle, args=(conn,), daemon=True).start()
''')
import subprocess
with ab.server("", cmd=[sys.executable, "tiny_http.py", "{port}"]) as base:
    for args in (["-s", f"{base}/hello?name=curl"],
                 ["-s", "-X", "POST", "-H", "Content-Type: application/json", "-d", '{"a": [1, 2]}', f"{base}/echo"],
                 ["-s", "-i", "-X", "DELETE", f"{base}/hello"]):
        out = subprocess.run(["curl", *args], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
        print("curl", " ".join(a for a in args if a not in ("-s",)).replace(base, ""), "->",
              ab.mask(out).replace("\r\n", " | ").strip())
    print(httpx.post(f"{base}/echo", content=b"{bad").status_code,
          httpx.get(f"{base}/nope").status_code,
          httpx.post(f"{base}/echo", json={"k": "v"}).json())
    with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", int(base.rsplit(":", 1)[1]))) as s:   # POST without length
        s.sendall(b"POST /echo HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n")
        print(s.recv(200).split(b"\r\n")[0].decode())
```
Seventy lines handle the cases that matter for an API: routing by path, then
by method (405 with `Allow`), framing by `Content-Length` (411 when it is
missing), and validation (400). What is missing is as instructive: no
keep-alive or pipelining, no chunked bodies, no limits on header or body size
(a client announcing `Content-Length: 10000000000` would make the thread wait
for ever — real servers cap sizes and use timeouts), no TLS. This is why one
writes the application with a framework (@sec-api-endpoints) and leaves the
protocol to a battle-tested server such as uvicorn.
:::

## HTTP methods: safety, idempotence and retries {#sec-api-methods}

### The methods and their semantics

The **method** of a request says what the client wants done with the target
resource. RFC 9110 defines the semantics of each, and two properties that
clients, proxies and caches rely on [@rfc9110, §9.2]:

- a method is **safe** if the client does not request any change of state
  on the server — it is essentially read-only (the server may still log the
  request);
- a method is **idempotent** if the intended effect on the server of several
  identical requests is the same as that of one.

| Method | Purpose | Safe | Idempotent | Typical success |
|---|---|:---:|:---:|---|
| `GET` | read a representation of the resource | ✓ | ✓ | 200 |
| `HEAD` | as `GET`, headers only | ✓ | ✓ | 200 |
| `OPTIONS` | which methods/options the resource supports | ✓ | ✓ | 200, 204 |
| `PUT` | create or **replace** the resource with the representation sent | | ✓ | 200, 201, 204 |
| `DELETE` | remove the resource | | ✓ | 200, 204 |
| `POST` | let the resource **process** the representation (often: create a new subordinate resource) | | | 201 + `Location`, 200, 202 |
| `PATCH` | apply a set of **changes** to the resource [@rfc5789] | | | 200, 204 |

Idempotence is about *effect*, not about the *response*: a second `DELETE`
of the same resource typically returns 404, but the state — resource absent
— is the same as after the first. `PATCH` is not idempotent in general
(`{"op": "add", "path": "/stock", "value": 1}` adds every time), although a
particular patch may be.

::: {#def-api-idempotent}
## Idempotent operation
Let $S$ be the set of states of the server. An operation with effect $f : S
\to S$ is **idempotent** if $f \circ f = f$, i.e. $f(f(s)) = f(s)$ for every
state $s$. It is **safe** if $f$ is the identity.
:::

::: {#prp-api-idempotent-power}
## Repeating an idempotent request
If $f$ is idempotent, then $f^n = f$ for every $n \ge 1$. The composition of
two idempotent operations, however, is not idempotent in general.
:::

*In one line:* one idempotent request can be repeated any number of times,
but a *sequence* of idempotent requests cannot be replayed as a block.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-api-idempotent-power
By induction: $f^1 = f$; if $f^n = f$ then $f^{n+1} = f \circ f^n = f
\circ f = f$. For the second claim take states $(a, b)$ of two integer
resources, $f$: "`PUT` $a := b$" and $g$: "`PUT` $b := a + 1$". Both are
idempotent ($f$ leaves $a = b$, and applying it again changes nothing; $g$
sets $b$ from the unchanged $a$). But $h = g \circ f$ maps $(0, 0) \mapsto (0,
1)$ and then $(0, 1) \mapsto (1, 2)$: $h \circ h \ne h$. $\blacksquare$
:::

### Retries

Networks lose messages, servers restart, gateways time out. A client that
gets no response — or a 502, 503, 504 — cannot tell whether the request was
**not performed** or **performed but the response was lost**. The standard
answer is to retry.

::: {#thm-api-retry}
## Success with retries
If each attempt succeeds independently with probability $p$, then at least one
of $n$ attempts succeeds with probability
$$
1 - (1 - p)^n ,
$$ {#eq-api-retry}
and $n \ge \log\varepsilon/\log(1 - p)$ attempts make the probability of
total failure at most $\varepsilon$.
:::

*In one line:* independent failures multiply — three attempts at 90 % each
fail together only once in a thousand.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-api-retry
All $n$ attempts fail with probability $\prod_{k=1}^n(1 - p) = (1 - p)^n$ by
independence; the complement is @eq-api-retry. $(1 - p)^n \le \varepsilon$
if and only if $n\log(1 - p) \le \log\varepsilon$; dividing by $\log(1 - p) <
0$ reverses the inequality. $\blacksquare$
:::

The hypothesis of **independence** is the weak point. Failures are
correlated in time: a server that is down at one instant is probably down a
moment later, and retrying immediately mostly measures the same outage. If
the outage lasts $D$ seconds, attempts spaced by much less than $D$ are not
independent at all; spacing them out — **backoff** — is what makes the formula
approximately true. And retries have a cost: every failed attempt is load on a
server that may be failing *because* of load.

Retrying is safe only if repeating the request is harmless.

::: {#thm-api-exactly-once}
## At least once + idempotent = exactly-once effect
Suppose that (H1) the server applies the effect $f$ of a request at least once
and finitely many times — the client retries until it gets a response, and
duplicates may reach the server; (H2) $f$ is idempotent; (H3) no other
operation changes the affected state between the first and the last
application of $f$. Then the final state is $f(s)$, as if the request had been
applied exactly once.
:::

*In one line:* idempotence turns "at least once", which networks can
guarantee, into "exactly once", which they cannot — provided duplicates do
not interleave with other writes.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-api-exactly-once
By (H1) the request is applied $k \ge 1$ times; by (H3) these applications
are consecutive in the sequence of operations on the state, which therefore
goes from $s$ to $f^k(s)$; by (H2) and @prp-api-idempotent-power, $f^k(s) =
f(s)$. $\blacksquare$

Hypothesis (H3) is not a formality. A `PUT x = 1` delayed in the network,
followed by a `PUT x = 2` from another client and then by the duplicate of
the first, ends with $x = 1$: each operation is idempotent, yet the outcome
is not that of any order in which each was applied once. Conditional
requests (`If-Match`, @sec-api-rest) or idempotency keys with a bounded
validity close this gap.
:::

`POST` is not idempotent: retrying "create an order" may create two. The
standard remedy is an **idempotency key**: the client generates a unique
value for each *logical* operation and sends it in a header
(`Idempotency-Key: 8e03978e-…`, an IETF draft standardising a widespread
practice [@jena2025]); the server records the key with the response and, when
the key comes again, returns the recorded response without acting again. The
effect of a request becomes a function of the pair (state, store of keys),
and it is idempotent: the first application acts and records, the next ones
find the record. @exr-api1-methods-medium demonstrates it.

### Backoff and jitter

When many clients fail at the same moment — the server restarted, a
network partition healed — and all retry after the same delay, they arrive
together again, overload the server again, fail again: a **thundering herd**.
Two ideas break the cycle [@brooker2015]:

- **exponential backoff**: wait longer after each failure, $w_k = \min(C,
  b\,2^k)$ before the retry $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$ ($b$ the base delay, $C$ a
  cap), so that the offered load decreases geometrically;
- **jitter**: wait a *random* time — **full jitter** draws the wait uniformly
  in $[0, w_k]$, **equal jitter** waits $w_k/2$ plus a uniform draw in $[0,
  w_k/2]$ — so that clients desynchronise.

::: {#prp-api-jitter}
## Expected waits and the spread of the herd
(i) The expected wait before retry $k$ is $w_k$ without jitter, $w_k/2$ with
full jitter and $3w_k/4$ with equal jitter; the expected time until retry $n$
is the sum of the expected waits.
(ii) If $N$ clients fail at the same instant, without jitter all their first
retries arrive at the same instant $w_0$; with full jitter they are
independent and uniform on $[0, w_0]$, so the expected number arriving in any
window of length $\delta \le w_0$ is $N\delta/w_0$.
:::

*In one line:* jitter costs at most a constant factor in waiting (it even
halves the mean wait) and turns a spike of $N$ simultaneous requests into a
flow of $N/w_0$ requests per second.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-api-jitter
(i) The mean of a uniform variable on $[a, a + \ell]$ is $a + \ell/2$:
$w_k/2$ for $[0, w_k]$ and $w_k/2 + w_k/4 = 3w_k/4$ for $[w_k/2, w_k]$.
The time until retry $n$ is a sum of waits (plus response times), and the
expectation of a sum is the sum of the expectations. (ii) Each arrival time
$U_i$ is uniform on $[0, w_0]$, so $P(U_i \in [t, t + \delta]) = \delta/w_0$
for a window inside $[0, w_0]$; the number of arrivals in the window is a sum
of $N$ indicators, with expectation $N\delta/w_0$. $\blacksquare$
:::

The widget simulates 200 clients that fail together at time 0 against a
server that can serve 10 requests per 100 ms; each failed request retries
with the chosen policy.

::: {.widget}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof boPolicy = Inputs.radio(["no backoff", "exponential, no jitter", "exponential, full jitter", "exponential, equal jitter"],
                               {value: "exponential, no jitter", label: "retry policy"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
boSim = {
  // 200 clients, capacity 10 requests per 100 ms slot, base 100 ms, cap 6.4 s, 12 attempts at most
  let seed = 7; const rnd = () => (seed = (seed * 16807) % 2147483647) / 2147483647;
  const N = 200, cap = 10, slot = 100, base = 100, maxw = 6400, horizon = 12000;
  let pending = Array.from({length: N}, () => ({t: 0, k: 0}));
  const load = new Map(); let calls = 0, done = 0, lastDone = 0;
  while (pending.length) {
    pending.sort((a, b) => a.t - b.t);
    const bins = new Map(); const next = [];
    for (const c of pending) {
      if (c.t > horizon) continue;
      const s = Math.floor(c.t / slot); bins.set(s, (bins.get(s) || 0) + 1); calls++;
      load.set(s, (load.get(s) || 0) + 1);
      if (bins.get(s) <= cap) { done++; lastDone = Math.max(lastDone, c.t); continue; }
      if (c.k >= 11) continue;
      const w = boPolicy === "no backoff" ? slot : Math.min(maxw, base * 2 ** c.k);
      const wait = boPolicy.includes("full") ? rnd() * w : boPolicy.includes("equal") ? w / 2 + rnd() * w / 2 : w;
      next.push({t: c.t + Math.max(wait, 1), k: c.k + 1});
    }
    pending = next;
  }
  const rows = [...load.entries()].map(([s, n]) => ({t: s * slot / 1000, n}));
  return {rows, calls, done, lastDone};
}
```

```{ojs}

```

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-api1-methods-easy}
## Easy — which requests may be retried?
For each request say whether it is safe, idempotent, both or neither, and
whether a client may retry it blindly after a timeout: (a) `GET
/wines?colour=red`; (b) `PUT /wines/42` with a full representation; (c)
`DELETE /wines/42`; (d) `POST /wines` with a new wine; (e) `PATCH /stock/42`
with `{"delta": -1}`; (f) `PATCH /wines/42` with `{"alcohol": 13.5}`. Then
show with @prp-api-idempotent-power why the two-request sequence "(b) then
(f)" cannot be replayed as a unit in general, even though each request is
idempotent.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Write each effect as a function on the state. A patch that *sets* a field is
idempotent; one that *adds* is not.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) safe and idempotent: retry. (b) idempotent: retry. (c) idempotent:
retry (expect 404 on a repetition). (d) neither: retry only with an
idempotency key. (e) not idempotent (each application subtracts one): no
blind retry. (f) idempotent (it sets a value): retry. For the sequence:
replaying "(b) then (f)" as a block is safe here only because (b) replaces
the whole resource and (f) sets a field of it — the composition happens to be
idempotent; in general it is not, as the proof of @prp-api-idempotent-power
shows, and interleavings with other clients (H3) break even this case:
```{python}
state = {"alcohol": 12.0}
put_b = lambda s: {"alcohol": 13.0}                     # replace the resource
patch_f = lambda s: {**s, "alcohol": 13.5}             # set a field
other = lambda s: {**s, "alcohol": s["alcohol"] + 1}  # another client's non-idempotent update
once = patch_f(put_b(state))
print("once:", once, "| twice in a row:", patch_f(put_b(once)))
print("with another update in between, then a duplicate of (b):", put_b(other(once)))
```
The duplicate of (b) arriving late erases the other client's update — the
"lost update" that @sec-api-rest prevents with `If-Match`.
:::

::: {#exr-api1-methods-medium}
## Medium — duplicates and idempotency keys
Build a FastAPI service with `POST /orders` that creates an order with a new
ID. Write an httpx client that retries on transport errors, and connect it
through an `httpx.MockTransport` that forwards each request to the service but
**loses the response** of the first two attempts. Count the orders created.
Then add support for an `Idempotency-Key` header on the server and send one
key per logical order from the client; count again.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
The mock transport's handler receives an `httpx.Request`: forward it with a
`TestClient` (which talks to the app in-process), then raise
`httpx.ReadTimeout` if the response is to be "lost" — the server has acted,
the client does not know. On the server, keep a dictionary key → response.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from fastapi import FastAPI, Header
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
import itertools, uuid

def make_app():
    app = FastAPI()
    app.state.orders, app.state.seen = {}, {}
    ids = itertools.count(1)

    @app.post("/orders", status_code=201)
    def create(order: dict, idempotency_key: str | None = Header(default=None)):
        if idempotency_key in app.state.seen:                    # a retry: replay the recorded answer
            return app.state.seen[idempotency_key]
        oid = next(ids)
        app.state.orders[oid] = order
        result = {"id": oid, **order}
        if idempotency_key is not None:
            app.state.seen[idempotency_key] = result
        return result
    return app

def lossy(app, lose=2):
    inner, lost = TestClient(app), [0]
    def handler(request: httpx.Request):
        r = inner.request(request.method, str(request.url.path), content=request.content, headers=request.headers)
        if lost[0] < lose:                                        # the server acted, the reply is lost
            lost[0] += 1
            raise httpx.ReadTimeout("response lost", request=request)
        return httpx.Response(r.status_code, content=r.content, headers=r.headers)
    return httpx.MockTransport(handler)

def post_with_retries(client, body, key=None, attempts=5):
    headers = {"Idempotency-Key": key} if key else {}
    for k in range(attempts):
        try:
            return client.post("http://api/orders", json=body, headers=headers)
        except httpx.TransportError:
            continue
    raise RuntimeError("gave up")

for use_key in (False, True):
    app = make_app()
    with httpx.Client(transport=lossy(app)) as client:
        r = post_with_retries(client, {"wine": 42, "bottles": 6}, key=str(uuid.uuid4()) if use_key else None)
    print(f"idempotency key: {use_key!s:5}  -> response {r.status_code} {r.json()}, orders stored: {len(app.state.orders)}")
```
Without a key the client sees one successful response but the server holds
three orders — the two "lost" attempts were executed. With the key, the second
and third attempts find the recorded result and return it: one order, and the
same response the first attempt would have returned. In production the store
of keys must be shared by all replicas (a database, not a dictionary), have an
expiry, and be updated **atomically** with the effect — otherwise two
concurrent retries can both miss the key. Mistake to avoid: generating a new
key at each *attempt* instead of each *logical operation*, which makes the
key useless.
:::

::: {#exr-api1-methods-hard}
## Hard — a thundering herd
Simulate $N = 500$ clients whose requests all fail at time 0, against a server
that can serve $C = 20$ requests per 100 ms slot (requests beyond the
capacity of a slot fail). Compare four policies — immediate retry, exponential
backoff without jitter, with full jitter, with equal jitter (base 100 ms, cap
6.4 s) — on the time until all clients are served, the total number of
requests and the peak load. Check @prp-api-jitter(ii) on the first round.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
An event-driven simulation is enough: keep the time of each client's next
attempt, process slot by slot, serve the first $C$ attempts of each slot
(in random order among those of the slot) and reschedule the others with
their policy.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
def herd(policy, N=500, C=20, slot=0.1, base=0.1, cap=6.4, seed=0, horizon=120):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t = np.zeros(N); k = np.zeros(N, dtype=int); served = np.zeros(N, dtype=bool)
    calls, peak, finish, first_round = 0, 0, 0.0, None         # peak: largest slot load after time 0
    while not served.all():
        s = np.floor(t[~served].min() / slot)                  # next slot with attempts
        if s * slot > horizon:
            break
        idx = np.where(~served & (np.floor(t / slot) == s))[0]
        rng.shuffle(idx)
        calls += len(idx); peak = max(peak, len(idx) if s > 0 else 0)
        ok, fail = idx[:C], idx[C:]
        served[ok] = True; finish = (s + 1) * slot
        w = np.minimum(cap, base * 2.0 ** k[fail]) if policy != "immediate" else np.full(len(fail), slot)
        if policy == "full jitter":
            w = rng.uniform(0, w)
        elif policy == "equal jitter":
            w = w / 2 + rng.uniform(0, w / 2)
        if first_round is None and policy == "full jitter":
            first_round = s * slot + w                         # arrival times of the first retries
        t[fail] = s * slot + np.maximum(w, 1e-9) + 1e-9
        k[fail] += 1
    return finish, calls, peak, first_round

for pol in ("immediate", "no jitter", "full jitter", "equal jitter"):
    finish, calls, peak, fr = herd(pol)
    print(f"{pol:13s}: all served after {finish:5.1f} s, {calls:5d} requests ({calls / 500:.1f} per client), "
          f"largest retry burst {peak} in one slot")
fr = herd("full jitter")[3]
counts = np.histogram(fr, bins=np.arange(0, 0.1 + 1e-9, 0.01))[0]
print(f"first retries with full jitter: mean {counts.mean():.1f} per 10 ms window (formula {480 * 0.01 / 0.1:.0f})")
```
Immediate retries finish first — the server works at full capacity from the
first slot, 25 slots for 500 clients — but every client sends about 13
requests, twelve of them rejected: in this model a rejection is free, while a
real server spends resources on each one, so the useful work slows down
exactly when the server is overloaded. Backoff without jitter is the worst of
both worlds: the clients stay synchronised, each retry wave hits a single slot
that can serve only 20 of them, and the doubling delays stretch the recovery
to almost two minutes with as many requests as before. Full and equal jitter
spread the waves over time: everyone is served within a few seconds with
about five requests per client, less than half as many. Full jitter also
cuts the largest burst; equal jitter, whose first retries fall in a window
($[w_0/2, w_0]$) narrower than one slot of this server, still sends one large
burst early on — the reason Brooker's simulations favour full jitter. The first-round histogram
agrees with $N\delta/w_0$ for the 480 clients that failed at time 0.
Brooker's simulations reach the same conclusion and recommend full jitter
[@brooker2015]. In the direction of production: client libraries should cap
the number of retries and the total time (a *retry budget*), retry only 429,
502–504 and broken connections, honour `Retry-After`, and retry only
idempotent requests or requests with an idempotency key. Mistake to avoid:
adding jitter but resetting the exponent after every failure, which keeps
clients near the base delay.
:::

## REST: an architectural style for APIs {#sec-api-rest}

### Fielding's constraints

**REST** — *representational state transfer* — is not a protocol or a
format. It is the **architectural style** that Roy Fielding, one of the
authors of the HTTP/1.1 specification, extracted from the design of the Web
in his doctoral dissertation [@fielding2000, ch. 5]: a set of
**constraints** on how the components of a distributed system interact, each
chosen for the properties it brings — scalability, simplicity, evolvability,
reliability — at a stated cost.

| Constraint | What it requires | What it buys | What it costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| client–server | user interface separated from data and logic | the two sides evolve independently | — |
| **stateless** | each request carries everything needed to understand it; no session state on the server | any server replica can answer any request; failures are easy to recover; requests can be inspected in isolation | repeated data in every request |
| **cache** | responses say whether and for how long they may be reused | fewer requests, lower latency, less load | stale data, if the labels are wrong |
| **uniform interface** | resources identified by URIs; manipulated through representations; self-descriptive messages; hypermedia drives the application state | one generic interface for all resources: generic clients, proxies, caches | a standard form is less efficient than a custom one |
| layered system | each component sees only the next layer | proxies, gateways, load balancers, caches can be inserted | latency of the extra hops |
| code on demand (optional) | servers may send code to run on the client | extensible clients | visibility |

The central notion is the **resource**: any information that can be named —
a wine, the list of red wines, today's prediction for a batch, the current
version of a model. A resource is identified by a **URI** and manipulated
through **representations** of its state (a JSON document, a CSV file)
exchanged with the uniform methods of @sec-api-methods. The client does not
call "functions on the server"; it **transfers representations of resource
state**, which is where the name comes from.

Many APIs called "REST" satisfy only part of this — typically
resources-plus-methods with JSON, without hypermedia. That pragmatic subset
(level 2 of Richardson's maturity model [@fowler2010]) captures most of the
benefits for machine-to-machine APIs: uniform methods with known semantics,
status codes, caching, statelessness. The opposite style is **RPC over HTTP**
— `POST /getWine`, `POST /deleteWine` — which uses HTTP as a mere tunnel and
loses everything HTTP knows about safety, idempotence and caching.

**Hypermedia** — "the engine of application state" — means that responses
contain the links to the next possible actions, so that clients follow links
instead of building URLs from out-of-band knowledge. In HTTP APIs this is
done in the body (`"next": "/wines?after=42"`) or with the `Link` header
[@rfc8288], which carries typed links:

```http
Link: <https://api.example.com/v1/wines?after=42&limit=20>; rel="next",
      <https://api.example.com/v1/wines?limit=20>; rel="first"
```

### Caching

A **cache** stores responses and reuses them for later equivalent requests:
the browser's cache, a company proxy, a content-delivery network. The server
controls it with headers [@rfc9111]: `Cache-Control: max-age=600` (fresh for
600 seconds), `no-cache` (reuse only after checking with the server),
`no-store` (never store — for sensitive data), `private` (only the user's
own cache), plus `Date`, `Age` and the validators of the next subsection. A
stored response is **fresh** while its age is below its **freshness
lifetime** (`max-age`), and a cache serves fresh responses without contacting
the origin.

The difficulty is the **age**: the cache must estimate how long ago the
origin produced the response, although the clocks of the machines disagree
and the response may have waited in other caches. RFC 9111 specifies the
computation [@rfc9111, §4.2.3], with the request sent at `request_time` and
the response received at `response_time`, both by the cache's clock:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{apparent\_age} &= \max(0,\ \text{response\_time} - \text{date\_value}),\\
\text{corrected\_age\_value} &= \text{age\_value} + (\text{response\_time} - \text{request\_time}),\\
\text{corrected\_initial\_age} &= \max(\text{apparent\_age},\ \text{corrected\_age\_value}),\\
\text{current\_age} &= \text{corrected\_initial\_age} + (\text{now} - \text{response\_time}),
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-api-age}
where `date_value` is the `Date` header (the origin's clock) and `age_value`
the `Age` header (0 if absent).

::: {#thm-api-age}
## The computed age never underestimates the true age
Suppose that the origin generated the response at time $t_0$ and either its
`Date` header is accurate with respect to the cache's clock, or every cache
on the path reports in `Age` an upper bound of the time elapsed since $t_0$
when it forwarded the response. Then $\text{current\_age} \ge \text{now} -
t_0$: a response the cache judges fresh is never older than its freshness
lifetime claims.
:::

*In one line:* the two estimates guard against two different failures — a
wrong clock at the origin and time spent in other caches — and taking their
maximum, plus the whole round trip, errs only on the side of caution.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-api-age
It suffices to show $\text{corrected\_initial\_age} \ge \text{response\_time}
- t_0$ (the true age on arrival), since adding $\text{now} - \text{response\_time}$
to both sides gives the claim. If the `Date` is accurate, $\text{date\_value}
= t_0$ and $\text{apparent\_age} \ge \text{response\_time} - t_0$. Otherwise,
let $t_s$ be the time the last cache on the path sent the response; by
assumption $\text{age\_value} \ge t_s - t_0$ (with no intermediate cache,
$\text{age\_value} = 0$ and $t_s = t_0$). The response was sent after the
request was made, $t_s \ge \text{request\_time}$, so
$\text{corrected\_age\_value} \ge (t_s - t_0) + (\text{response\_time} - t_s) =
\text{response\_time} - t_0$. In both cases the maximum is at least the true
age. The price of the guarantee is that the whole round trip is counted, as
if the response had been produced at the moment of the request.
$\blacksquare$
:::

```{python}
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime

def current_age(headers, request_time, response_time, now):
    """Age in seconds per RFC 9111 §4.2.3 (times: seconds by the cache's clock)."""
    date_value = parsedate_to_datetime(headers["Date"]).timestamp()
    age_value = int(headers.get("Age", 0))
    apparent_age = max(0, response_time - date_value)
    corrected_age_value = age_value + (response_time - request_time)
    corrected_initial_age = max(apparent_age, corrected_age_value)
    return corrected_initial_age + (now - response_time)

def freshness_lifetime(headers):
    for directive in headers.get("Cache-Control", "").split(","):
        name, _, value = directive.strip().partition("=")
        if name == "max-age":
            return int(value)
    return 0

t0 = parsedate_to_datetime("Mon, 16 Nov 2026 10:00:00 GMT").timestamp()
h = {"Date": "Mon, 16 Nov 2026 10:00:00 GMT", "Age": "30", "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=120"}
age = current_age(h, request_time=t0 + 5, response_time=t0 + 7, now=t0 + 70)
print(f"current age {age:.0f} s, lifetime {freshness_lifetime(h)} s, fresh: {age < freshness_lifetime(h)}")
```

Here the response passed through a cache that held it 30 s (`Age: 30`), the
round trip took 2 s and the cache has held it for 63 s since: $\max(7, 32) +
63 = 95$ s, below the lifetime of 120 s.

### Conditional requests and validators

When a stored response is stale, or for data that must always be checked,
the client can **revalidate** instead of downloading again. The server labels
each representation with a **validator** — an **entity tag**, `ETag:
"a3f2…"`, an opaque string that changes whenever the representation changes
(often a hash of it), or `Last-Modified` — and the client sends it back in a
**conditional request** [@rfc9110, §13]:

- `If-None-Match: "a3f2…"` on a `GET`: if the tag still matches, the server
  answers **304 Not Modified** with no body — the client's copy is valid;
- `If-Match: "a3f2…"` on a `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`: the server applies
  the change **only if** the resource still has that tag, otherwise it answers
  **412 Precondition Failed**.

The second use solves a classic problem of concurrent editing, the **lost
update**: two clients read the same version, both modify it and write it
back; the second write silently erases the first.

::: {#thm-api-lost-update}
## Optimistic concurrency with `If-Match` prevents lost updates
Suppose that (i) the validator of a resource changes at every change of its
state (a strong `ETag`, or a version number), (ii) the server checks
`If-Match` and applies the write **atomically** (no other write between the
check and the write), and (iii) every client sends the validator of the
version it read. Then of all the writes based on the same version, at most one
succeeds, and every successful write replaces exactly the version its client
read: no update is overwritten without having been seen.
:::

*In one line:* `If-Match` is a compare-and-swap on the resource — "write
this, but only if nobody has written since I read" — and the loser learns it
(412) instead of silently winning.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-api-lost-update
Let $W_1$ and $W_2$ be two writes based on the same version, with validator
$v$, and say $W_1$ is applied first (writes are serialised by (ii)). When
$W_1$ succeeds the state changes, so by (i) the validator becomes $v' \ne v$.
When $W_2$ is checked, the current validator is $v'$ or a later one; none of
them equals $v$ (a validator that changes at every change never returns to an
earlier value if it is a version counter; for a hash, a return to $v$ would
mean the state returned exactly to the one $W_2$ read — then nothing $W_2$
saw was lost). So $W_2$ fails with 412. Consequently each successful write
was checked against the validator of the then-current version, which by
(iii) is the version its client read. $\blacksquare$
:::

The client that receives 412 must re-read, merge or ask the user, and try
again — the "optimistic" part: no locks are held between reading and
writing, and conflicts, assumed rare, are detected rather than prevented. Here
is a resource with tags, in FastAPI (introduced properly in
@sec-api-endpoints), exercised in-process with a `TestClient`:

```{python}
import hashlib
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response, HTTPException
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()
WINES = {42: {"id": 42, "name": "Barolo", "alcohol": 14.0}}

def etag_of(obj) -> str:
    return '"' + hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:16] + '"'

@app.get("/wines/{wine_id}")
def read_wine(wine_id: int, request: Request, response: Response):
    wine = WINES.get(wine_id) or None
    if wine is None:
        raise HTTPException(404)
    tag = etag_of(wine)
    if request.headers.get("if-none-match") == tag:
        return Response(status_code=304, headers={"ETag": tag})       # the client's copy is current
    response.headers["ETag"] = tag
    response.headers["Cache-Control"] = "no-cache"                    # store, but revalidate each time
    return wine

@app.put("/wines/{wine_id}")
def replace_wine(wine_id: int, wine: dict, request: Request, response: Response):
    current = WINES.get(wine_id)
    if current is not None and request.headers.get("if-match") not in (None, etag_of(current)):
        raise HTTPException(412, "the wine was modified since you read it")
    WINES[wine_id] = {**wine, "id": wine_id}
    response.headers["ETag"] = etag_of(WINES[wine_id])
    return WINES[wine_id]

client = TestClient(app)
r1 = client.get("/wines/42");  tag = r1.headers["etag"]
r2 = client.get("/wines/42", headers={"If-None-Match": tag})
print(r1.status_code, tag, r1.json(), "| revalidation:", r2.status_code, f"{len(r2.content)} bytes of body")
ok = client.put("/wines/42", json={"name": "Barolo", "alcohol": 14.5}, headers={"If-Match": tag})
stale = client.put("/wines/42", json={"name": "Barolo DOCG", "alcohol": 14.0}, headers={"If-Match": tag})
print("first writer:", ok.status_code, "| second writer with the old tag:", stale.status_code, stale.json())
```

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-api1-rest-easy}
## Easy — age and freshness by hand
A cache sends a request at 10:00:00 (its clock) and receives at 10:00:03 a
response with `Date: 09:59:30`, `Age: 10` and `Cache-Control:
max-age=60`. Compute with @eq-api-age the current age at 10:00:30 and at
10:01:00, and say whether the response is fresh. What changes if the origin's
clock is 40 s fast (`Date: 10:00:40`)?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Work in seconds after 10:00:00. A negative apparent age is clipped to 0.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
With times in seconds after 10:00:00: request 0, response 3, date $-30$,
age 10. Apparent age $\max(0, 3 + 30) = 33$; corrected age value $10 + 3 =
13$; initial age 33. At 10:00:30: $33 + 27 = 60$, not fresh ($60 \not< 60$);
at 10:01:00: 90, stale. With the fast clock: apparent age $\max(0, 3 - 40) =
0$, initial age $\max(0, 13) = 13$: at 10:00:30 the age is 40, fresh. The
`Age` header saved the computation from the wrong clock — the robustness that
@thm-api-age formalises.
```{python}
base = parsedate_to_datetime("Mon, 16 Nov 2026 10:00:00 GMT").timestamp()
for date in ("09:59:30", "10:00:40"):
    h = {"Date": f"Mon, 16 Nov 2026 {date} GMT", "Age": "10", "Cache-Control": "max-age=60"}
    for now in (30, 60):
        a = current_age(h, base, base + 3, base + now)
        print(f"Date {date}, now 10:00:{now:02d} -> age {a:.0f} s, fresh {a < freshness_lifetime(h)}"
              if now < 60 else f"Date {date}, now 10:01:00 -> age {a:.0f} s, fresh {a < freshness_lifetime(h)}")
```
The usual mistake is to compute the age as `now - Date` only, which trusts the
origin's clock and ignores the time spent in other caches.
:::

::: {#exr-api1-rest-medium}
## Medium — what revalidation saves
Serve a collection of 1 000 wines (about 100 kB of JSON) with an `ETag`.
Simulate a client that polls it every minute for an hour, while the
collection changes three times during the hour. Count the bytes of body
transferred with plain `GET`s and with conditional `GET`s
(`If-None-Match`), and the number of full downloads in each case.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
The client keeps the last `ETag` and body; on 304 it reuses the body. The
server must compute the tag from the current state (a version counter or a
hash).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
coll_app = FastAPI()
state = {"version": 1, "wines": [{"id": i, "alcohol": float(round(rng.uniform(11, 15), 1)),
                                  "colour": str(rng.choice(["red", "white", "rosé"]))} for i in range(1000)]}

@coll_app.get("/wines")
def list_wines(request: Request):
    tag = f'"v{state["version"]}"'                              # version counter as a strong validator
    if request.headers.get("if-none-match") == tag:
        return Response(status_code=304, headers={"ETag": tag})
    return Response(json.dumps(state["wines"]), media_type="application/json", headers={"ETag": tag})

cc = TestClient(coll_app)
changes = {13, 31, 47}                                          # minutes at which the collection changes
for conditional in (False, True):
    state["version"] = 1
    tag, body, transferred, full = None, None, 0, 0
    for minute in range(60):
        if minute in changes:
            state["version"] += 1
        headers = {"If-None-Match": tag} if conditional and tag else {}
        r = cc.get("/wines", headers=headers)
        transferred += len(r.content)
        if r.status_code == 200:
            tag, body, full = r.headers["etag"], r.content, full + 1
    print(f"{'conditional' if conditional else 'plain'} GETs: {full} full downloads, {transferred / 1e3:,.0f} kB of body")
```
Plain polling downloads the whole collection sixty times; conditional polling
downloads it four times (the first request and after each of the three
changes) and receives 56 empty 304 responses. The saving grows with the size
of the resource and the polling frequency. The requests still cost a round
trip each: if even that is too much, the server can push changes (webhooks,
server-sent events) instead. A frequent bug: computing the `ETag` from
something that does not change with the content (a timestamp of the process
start), which makes clients keep stale data.
:::

::: {#exr-api1-rest-hard}
## Hard — two editors and a lost update
Two editors increment the stock of a wine concurrently: each reads the
resource, adds the bottles it received, and writes back with `PUT`. Run 200
such updates from 8 threads against a uvicorn server (a) without
preconditions, (b) with `If-Match`, retrying on 412 after re-reading. Compare
the final stock with the expected one, and check the atomicity hypothesis of
@thm-api-lost-update by removing the lock around the check-and-write.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Use a version counter as `ETag`. With a threaded server (FastAPI runs plain
`def` endpoints in a thread pool) the check and the write must be under a
`threading.Lock`. A small `time.sleep` between check and write makes races
easy to observe.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
ab.write("stock_api.py", '''
    import os, threading, time
    from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response, HTTPException

    app = FastAPI()
    STATE = {"stock": 0, "version": 0}
    LOCK = threading.Lock() if os.environ.get("ATOMIC", "1") == "1" else None

    @app.get("/stock")
    def read(response: Response):
        response.headers["ETag"] = f'"{STATE["version"]}"'
        return {"stock": STATE["stock"]}

    def check_and_write(if_match, new):
        if if_match is not None and if_match != f'"{STATE["version"]}"':
            raise HTTPException(412, "modified since read")
        time.sleep(0.001)                                    # widen the race window
        STATE["stock"], STATE["version"] = new, STATE["version"] + 1

    @app.put("/stock")
    def write(body: dict, request: Request):
        if LOCK:
            with LOCK:
                check_and_write(request.headers.get("if-match"), body["stock"])
        else:
            check_and_write(request.headers.get("if-match"), body["stock"])
        return {"stock": STATE["stock"]}
''')
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def editor(base, n, use_if_match):
    with httpx.Client(base_url=base) as c:
        conflicts = 0
        for _ in range(n):
            while True:
                r = c.get("/stock")
                headers = {"If-Match": r.headers["etag"]} if use_if_match else {}
                w = c.put("/stock", json={"stock": r.json()["stock"] + 1}, headers=headers)
                if w.status_code != 412:
                    break
                conflicts += 1                                 # someone wrote first: re-read and retry
        return conflicts

for label, use_if_match, atomic in (("(a) no precondition", False, "1"),
                                     ("(b) If-Match, atomic check", True, "1"),
                                     ("(b') If-Match, no lock", True, "0")):
    with ab.server("stock_api:app", env={"ATOMIC": atomic}) as base:
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as ex:
            conflicts = sum(ex.map(lambda _: editor(base, 25, use_if_match), range(8)))
        final = httpx.get(f"{base}/stock").json()["stock"]
    print(f"{label:28s}: final stock {final:3d} of 200 expected, {conflicts:4d} conflicts (412) handled")
```
Without preconditions most increments are lost: two editors read the same
stock and both write "stock + 1". With `If-Match` and an atomic check every
increment survives — the losers of each race get 412, re-read and try again,
which is the price of optimism under heavy contention. Without the lock, two
writes based on the same version can both pass the check before either
writes, and updates are lost again: the theorem's atomicity hypothesis is
essential, and in a real service it is provided by the database (a
conditional `UPDATE … WHERE version = ?` and a check that one row changed).
The cleaner design for this particular resource would avoid read-modify-write
altogether: an operation `POST /stock/movements {"delta": +1}` whose effect
is applied by the server atomically — at the cost of losing idempotence, so
it needs an idempotency key (@sec-api-methods).
:::

## Endpoints: design, validation and documentation {#sec-api-endpoints}

### What an endpoint is

An **endpoint** is one operation of an API: a **method** together with a
**URI template** — `GET /v1/wines/{wine_id}` — and the contract that goes
with it: path parameters (`wine_id`), query parameters (`?colour=red`),
headers, the request body, and for each outcome the status code and the
response body. The design rules that follow from the previous sections:

- **nouns, not verbs**: the method is the verb (`DELETE /wines/42`, not
  `POST /deleteWine?id=42`);
- **collections and items**: `/wines` (the collection: `GET` lists, `POST`
  creates) and `/wines/{id}` (an item: `GET`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`);
  sub-resources for containment, `/wines/{id}/reviews`;
- **query parameters** for filtering, sorting and pagination of collections;
- a **version** in the path (`/v1/…`) or in a header, changed only for
  incompatible changes;
- the **status code** that says what happened:

| Operation | Success | Typical failures |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /wines` | **201 Created** + `Location: /wines/{new id}` + the new resource | 409 (conflicts with an existing one), 422 (invalid) |
| `GET /wines/{id}` | 200 + representation | 404 |
| `PUT /wines/{id}` | 200 (or 204); 201 if it created the resource | 412 (precondition), 422 |
| `PATCH /wines/{id}` | 200 (or 204) | 404, 409, 422 |
| `DELETE /wines/{id}` | **204 No Content** | 404 |
| `GET /wines?colour=red&limit=20` | 200 + page + link to the next page | 400/422 (bad parameters) |

### Implementing endpoints with FastAPI

**FastAPI** [@ramirez2026] builds an API from typed Python functions: the
types of the parameters say where each value comes from (path, query, body)
and how to validate it, using **Pydantic** models [@pydantic2026]; invalid
requests are rejected with 422 before the function runs; and the whole API is
described automatically in OpenAPI. A complete CRUD for wines:

```{python}
from typing import Literal
from fastapi import status
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class WineIn(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=80)
    colour: Literal["red", "white", "rosé"]
    alcohol: float = Field(ge=5, le=20, description="% vol")
    year: int | None = Field(default=None, ge=1900, le=2100)

class Wine(WineIn):
    id: int

api = FastAPI(title="Wine catalogue", version="1.0")
DB: dict[int, Wine] = {}

@api.post("/v1/wines", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED, response_model=Wine)
def create_wine(wine: WineIn, response: Response):
    if any(w.name == wine.name for w in DB.values()):
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_409_CONFLICT, f"a wine named {wine.name!r} exists")
    new = Wine(id=max(DB, default=0) + 1, **wine.model_dump())
    DB[new.id] = new
    response.headers["Location"] = f"/v1/wines/{new.id}"
    return new

@api.get("/v1/wines/{wine_id}", response_model=Wine)
def get_wine(wine_id: int):
    if wine_id not in DB:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND, "no such wine")
    return DB[wine_id]

@api.get("/v1/wines", response_model=list[Wine])
def list_wines(colour: Literal["red", "white", "rosé"] | None = None, limit: int = 20):
    return [w for w in DB.values() if colour is None or w.colour == colour][:limit]

@api.delete("/v1/wines/{wine_id}", status_code=status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT)
def delete_wine(wine_id: int):
    if DB.pop(wine_id, None) is None:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND, "no such wine")

c = TestClient(api)
r = c.post("/v1/wines", json={"name": "Barolo", "colour": "red", "alcohol": 14.0, "year": 2019})
print(r.status_code, r.headers["location"], r.json())
c.post("/v1/wines", json={"name": "Soave", "colour": "white", "alcohol": 12.0})
print(c.get("/v1/wines", params={"colour": "white"}).json())
print(c.post("/v1/wines", json={"name": "Barolo", "colour": "red", "alcohol": 14.0}).status_code,
      c.delete("/v1/wines/1").status_code, c.get("/v1/wines/1").status_code)
bad = c.post("/v1/wines", json={"name": "", "colour": "blue", "alcohol": 45})
print(bad.status_code, [(e["loc"][-1], e["msg"]) for e in bad.json()["detail"]])
```

The `TestClient` calls the application in-process through the same HTTP
interface a network client would use, which makes it the natural tool for
**tests** of an API: every request above is a test case. The invalid request
was rejected with **422** and one error per field, generated from the type
annotations alone.

### Schemas: JSON Schema and OpenAPI

Each Pydantic model has a **JSON Schema** — the standard vocabulary for
describing and validating JSON documents, whose current version is 2020-12
[@wright2022] — and any other program, in any language, can validate against
it:

```{python}
from jsonschema import Draft202012Validator

schema = WineIn.model_json_schema()
print(json.dumps(schema["properties"]["alcohol"]), "| required:", schema["required"])
validator = Draft202012Validator(schema)
for doc in ({"name": "Soave", "colour": "white", "alcohol": 12.0},
            {"name": "Soave", "colour": "white", "alcohol": "twelve"}):
    errors = [e.message for e in validator.iter_errors(doc)]
    print("valid" if not errors else f"invalid: {errors}")
```

The whole API is described by an **OpenAPI** document — paths, methods,
parameters, schemas of bodies and responses, status codes — which FastAPI
generates and serves at `/openapi.json` (with interactive documentation at
`/docs`). The OpenAPI Specification is maintained by the OpenAPI Initiative;
its latest version is 3.2.0 (September 2025), and since 3.1 its schemas are
JSON Schema 2020-12 [@openapi2025]. FastAPI `{python} __import__("fastapi").__version__`
emits OpenAPI `{python} api.openapi()["openapi"]`:

```{python}
spec = api.openapi()
print("OpenAPI", spec["openapi"], "|", spec["info"]["title"], spec["info"]["version"])
for path, ops in spec["paths"].items():
    for method, op in ops.items():
        print(f"  {method.upper():6s} {path:22s} responses {sorted(op['responses'])}")
```

From this document one can generate client libraries, mock servers, tests,
and validate requests and responses in a gateway — the contract of the API,
in a form that machines can check.

### Errors that clients can rely on

Every API returns errors; a good one returns them in **one documented
format**. RFC 9457, *Problem Details for HTTP APIs* [@rfc9457], defines it:
a JSON object with media type `application/problem+json` and the members
`type` (a URI identifying the kind of problem), `title`, `status`, `detail`
and `instance`, plus any extension members. A client can then handle all
errors with the same code. @exr-api1-problem applies it to FastAPI.

### Pagination

A collection can be too long to return at once; the client asks for it in
**pages**. Two schemes are common.

- **Offset pagination**: `?offset=40&limit=20` returns the items in positions
  40–59 of the ordered collection. Simple, and the client can jump to any
  page.
- **Keyset (cursor) pagination**: `?after=K&limit=20` returns the first 20
  items whose sort key is greater than $K$, the key of the last item already
  received; the response carries the next cursor (or a `Link: rel="next"`)
  [@winand2012].

::: {#thm-api-pagination}
## Offsets skip and repeat; keysets do not
Let the items be totally ordered by a **unique, immutable** key, and let a
client traverse the collection page by page while other clients insert and
delete items.
(i) With offset pagination, an insertion of an item before the current offset
between two page requests makes the next page start with an item already
received (a duplicate); a deletion before the offset makes the next page skip
an item never received.
(ii) With keyset pagination, every item that is present during the whole
traversal is received exactly once, and items are received in increasing key
order, so no item is ever received twice.
:::

*In one line:* an offset counts positions, which move when the collection
changes; a key names a place in the order, which does not.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-api-pagination
(i) Suppose the client has received positions $0, \dots, m - 1$ and an item
is inserted at a position $j < m$. Every item from $j$ on moves one position
later: the item that was at position $m - 1$ (received) is now at $m$, the
first position of the next page — a duplicate. A deletion at $j < m$ moves
every later item one position earlier: the item that was at $m$ (not yet
received) is now at $m - 1$ and is never requested — a skip.

(ii) Let $K_0 = -\infty$ and $K_p$ the key of the last item of page $p$. Page
$p + 1$ contains the smallest keys $> K_p$ present at the time of the request;
keys are unique and every received key exceeds the previous cursor, so the
sequence of received keys is strictly increasing — no duplicates. Let $x$ be
present throughout, with key $k$. Let $p$ be the last page with $K_p < k$
(it exists since $K_0 = -\infty$, and the traversal ends only when a page is
not full, i.e. when no key $> K_p$ was left). Page $p + 1$ consists of the
smallest keys $> K_p$ at that time; $x$ is among the candidates, and either
it is returned or the page is full with keys smaller than $k$, so $K_{p+1} <
k$, contradicting the choice of $p$. So $x$ is on page $p + 1$. $\blacksquare$
:::

Keyset pagination is also **faster** on large tables: with an index on the
key, `WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT 20` reads 20 rows wherever the page is,
while `OFFSET 900000` must walk 900 000 rows to skip them
(@exr-api1-endpoints-hard). Its limits: no "jump to page 37", and the sort key
must be unique (append the ID to a non-unique sort key: `(price, id)`).

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-api1-endpoints-easy}
## Easy — from RPC to resources
Redesign these RPC-style endpoints as resources and methods, with the success
status code of each: `POST /getWine {"id": 42}`, `POST /createWine`, `GET
/deleteWine?id=42`, `POST /updateWineAlcohol {"id": 42, "alcohol": 13.5}`,
`GET /listRedWines`, `POST /searchWines {"text": "barolo"}`, `POST
/predictCultivar {"features": [...]}`. Which of the original endpoints were
*dangerous*, and why?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Think about what a crawler, a prefetching browser or a cache would do with a
`GET` that deletes. A prediction is the result of applying a model to an
input: is it a resource?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
| RPC | Resource + method | Success |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /getWine {"id": 42}` | `GET /v1/wines/42` | 200 |
| `POST /createWine` | `POST /v1/wines` | 201 + `Location` |
| `GET /deleteWine?id=42` | `DELETE /v1/wines/42` | 204 |
| `POST /updateWineAlcohol` | `PATCH /v1/wines/42 {"alcohol": 13.5}` | 200 |
| `GET /listRedWines` | `GET /v1/wines?colour=red` | 200 |
| `POST /searchWines` | `GET /v1/wines?q=barolo` | 200 |
| `POST /predictCultivar` | `POST /v1/predictions` (creates a prediction) or `POST /v1/models/wine/predict` | 200 or 201 |

`GET /deleteWine` is dangerous: `GET` is declared safe, so crawlers,
link-preview bots and prefetching browsers may call it, and caches may
replay it — any of them can delete wines. `POST /getWine` is wasteful rather
than dangerous: reads become uncacheable and non-retryable for every
intermediary. Predictions are the one place where a verb-like endpoint is
customary: the computation is safe and idempotent for a fixed model, but the
input is too large and structured for a query string, so `POST` is used — and
the response can be marked cacheable only by an application cache keyed on
the input.
:::

::: {#exr-api1-endpoints-medium}
## Medium — a CRUD with the right status codes
Extend the wine API with `PUT /v1/wines/{id}` (create or replace: 201 if it
created, 200 if it replaced) and `PATCH /v1/wines/{id}` (partial update; 404
if absent; 422 on invalid values; 409 if renaming to an existing name). Write
a test suite with `TestClient` that checks the status code, the headers and
the body of every success and failure case of the five endpoints.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
For `PATCH`, a second Pydantic model with every field optional, and
`model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` to apply only the fields sent; validate the
merged result with `Wine.model_validate`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import ValidationError

class WinePatch(BaseModel):
    name: Optional[str] = Field(default=None, min_length=1, max_length=80)
    colour: Optional[Literal["red", "white", "rosé"]] = None
    alcohol: Optional[float] = Field(default=None, ge=5, le=20)
    year: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, ge=1900, le=2100)

def name_taken(name, except_id):
    return any(w.name == name and w.id != except_id for w in DB.values())

@api.put("/v1/wines/{wine_id}", response_model=Wine)
def put_wine(wine_id: int, wine: WineIn, response: Response):
    if name_taken(wine.name, wine_id):
        raise HTTPException(409, "name already used")
    created = wine_id not in DB
    DB[wine_id] = Wine(id=wine_id, **wine.model_dump())
    response.status_code = 201 if created else 200
    if created:
        response.headers["Location"] = f"/v1/wines/{wine_id}"
    return DB[wine_id]

@api.patch("/v1/wines/{wine_id}", response_model=Wine)
def patch_wine(wine_id: int, patch: WinePatch):
    if wine_id not in DB:
        raise HTTPException(404, "no such wine")
    changes = patch.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
    if "name" in changes and name_taken(changes["name"], wine_id):
        raise HTTPException(409, "name already used")
    DB[wine_id] = Wine.model_validate({**DB[wine_id].model_dump(), **changes})
    return DB[wine_id]

DB.clear()
t = TestClient(api)
cases = [
    ("POST",   "/v1/wines",   {"name": "Barolo", "colour": "red", "alcohol": 14.0}, 201),
    ("POST",   "/v1/wines",   {"name": "Barolo", "colour": "red", "alcohol": 14.0}, 409),
    ("POST",   "/v1/wines",   {"name": "X", "colour": "green", "alcohol": 14.0}, 422),
    ("GET",    "/v1/wines/1", None, 200),
    ("GET",    "/v1/wines/9", None, 404),
    ("PUT",    "/v1/wines/7", {"name": "Soave", "colour": "white", "alcohol": 12.0}, 201),
    ("PUT",    "/v1/wines/7", {"name": "Soave", "colour": "white", "alcohol": 12.5}, 200),
    ("PATCH",  "/v1/wines/7", {"alcohol": 13.0}, 200),
    ("PATCH",  "/v1/wines/7", {"alcohol": 99}, 422),
    ("PATCH",  "/v1/wines/7", {"name": "Barolo"}, 409),
    ("PATCH",  "/v1/wines/8", {"alcohol": 13.0}, 404),
    ("DELETE", "/v1/wines/7", None, 204),
    ("DELETE", "/v1/wines/7", None, 404),
]
failures = 0
for method, path, body, expected in cases:
    r = t.request(method, path, json=body)
    ok = r.status_code == expected
    if method in ("POST", "PUT") and expected == 201:
        ok &= r.headers.get("location") == f"/v1/wines/{r.json()['id']}"
    if expected == 204:
        ok &= r.content == b""
    failures += not ok
    print(f"{'ok  ' if ok else 'FAIL'} {method:6s} {path:12s} -> {r.status_code}")
print("failures:", failures)
```
Each line is a test a CI pipeline can run in milliseconds, without a
network. The design decisions worth noticing: `PUT` to a client-chosen URI is
the idempotent way to create (retrying it is harmless), `POST` to the
collection is the non-idempotent one; `PATCH` validates the *merged* state,
not only the fields sent, so it cannot produce an invalid wine; 204 has no
body. A common error is answering 200 with `{"error": ...}` in the body:
every generic client, cache and monitoring tool then counts a failure as a
success.
:::

::: {#exr-api1-endpoints-hard}
## Hard — pagination that survives concurrent inserts
Store 1 000 000 wines in SQLite (standard library), with an integer primary
key. Implement `GET /v1/wines?limit=…&offset=…` and `GET
/v1/wines?limit=…&after=…` (the latter with a `Link: <…>; rel="next"`
header). (a) While a client walks the collection in pages of 100 items (the
first 5 000 items), insert a new item at the front before each page and
verify @thm-api-pagination: count duplicates and skips for both schemes.
(b) Time the retrieval of a page deep in the collection (offset 900 000) with
both schemes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
To insert "at the front" of an ordering by ID, order by ID **descending**
(newest first, as feeds do) and insert items with increasing IDs. For the
keyset query on a descending order the condition is `id < ?`. Use
`executemany` to fill the table quickly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
import sqlite3, threading
from urllib.parse import urlencode

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", check_same_thread=False)
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE wine (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, alcohol REAL)")
conn.executemany("INSERT INTO wine VALUES (?, ?)", ((i, 11 + (i % 40) / 10) for i in range(1, 1_000_001)))
db_lock = threading.Lock()

pages = FastAPI()

@pages.get("/v1/wines")
def wines(response: Response, limit: int = 100, offset: int | None = None, after: int | None = None):
    with db_lock:
        if after is None:                                       # offset pagination (newest first)
            rows = conn.execute("SELECT id, alcohol FROM wine ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ? OFFSET ?",
                                (limit, offset or 0)).fetchall()
        else:                                                   # keyset pagination
            rows = conn.execute("SELECT id, alcohol FROM wine WHERE id < ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?",
                                (after, limit)).fetchall()
    if after is not None or offset is None:
        if len(rows) == limit:
            response.headers["Link"] = f'</v1/wines?{urlencode({"limit": limit, "after": rows[-1][0]})}>; rel="next"'
    return [{"id": i, "alcohol": a} for i, a in rows]

pc = TestClient(pages)
next_id = 1_000_001

def insert_front():
    global next_id
    with db_lock:
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO wine VALUES (?, 12.5)", (next_id,)); next_id += 1

def walk(scheme, n_pages=50):
    seen, url = [], "/v1/wines?limit=100&after=" + str(10 ** 9) if scheme == "keyset" else None
    for p in range(n_pages):
        if scheme == "offset":
            r = pc.get("/v1/wines", params={"limit": 100, "offset": 100 * p})
        else:
            r = pc.get(url); url = r.headers["link"].split(">")[0][1:]
        seen += [w["id"] for w in r.json()]
        insert_front()                                          # someone inserts between two pages
    return seen

for scheme in ("offset", "keyset"):
    first = next_id                                             # items inserted from now on are "new"
    ids = walk(scheme)
    old = [i for i in ids if i < first]
    dup = len(old) - len(set(old))
    expected = set(range(min(old), max(old) + 1))              # every pre-existing item in the range walked
    print(f"{scheme:6s}: {len(ids)} items received, {dup} duplicates, {len(expected - set(old))} pre-existing items skipped")

import time as _t
queries = {"offset 900000": ("SELECT id, alcohol FROM wine ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 100 OFFSET 900000", ()),
           "keyset after id 100500": ("SELECT id, alcohol FROM wine WHERE id < ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 100", (100_500,))}
params = {"offset 900000": {"limit": 100, "offset": 900_000}, "keyset after id 100500": {"limit": 100, "after": 100_500}}
for label, (sql, args) in queries.items():
    s = _t.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(20):
        conn.execute(sql, args).fetchall()
    q_ms = 1000 * (_t.perf_counter() - s) / 20
    s = _t.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(20):
        pc.get("/v1/wines", params=params[label])
    print(f"{label:24s}: query {q_ms:6.2f} ms, whole request {1000 * (_t.perf_counter() - s) / 20:6.1f} ms")
```
(a) With offsets, every insertion at the front shifts the collection by one,
so each new page begins with the last item of the previous one: 49
duplicates in 50 pages, exactly as part (i) of the theorem predicts (with
deletions the error would be skips). With the keyset cursor no item is
received twice. In both schemes no pre-existing item was skipped, as the
theorem says for insertions (skips come from deletions); the new items,
inserted before the cursor, are not part of the keyset traversal — a client
